Neonates of the Red collared dove typically emerge from eggs incubated at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], a thermal regime that supports successful hatching after 12.5 days [ab = 12.5 days]. The initial wet weight at hatching is remarkably modest, recorded at just 5.8 grams [Ww0 = 5.8 grams], a value that underscores the altricial state of the newly emerged chick. This small size necessitates intensive parental brooding and frequent crop-milk provisioning during the early nestling phase. The energetic demands placed on the parents are substantial, as the nestling must more than double its body mass within the first week to sustain rapid feather development and thermoregulatory capacity. Field observations indicate that brooding adults maintain a nearly constant contact with the chick during the initial days post-hatch, a behaviour critical for temperature regulation given the altricial condition of the young. Comparative data from other members of the genus Streptopelia suggest that this hatching mass is near the lower end of the range, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes a rapid onset of parental provisioning over prolonged yolk investment in the egg.

Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight, occurs at 15.5 days after hatching [tx = 15.5 days after hatching], a relatively brief interval that places the Red collared dove among the faster-developing members of the Columbidae family at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This rapid fledging period is likely an adaptation to the species' preference for edge habitats, where nest predation pressure can be high, favouring a strategy that minimizes the duration of nest vulnerability. The emerging fledgling, though capable of short flights, remains dependent on parental provisioning for several more days while its flight muscles and foraging skills develop fully. This period of post-fledging care is energetically costly for the adults, who must simultaneously maintain their own body condition and prepare for subsequent breeding attempts within the same season. The timing of this milestone is closely tied to the thermal environment, as cooler conditions can delay feather maturation.

Sexual maturation in the Red collared dove, assessed under the same thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], is first achieved at 46 days after hatching [tp = 46 days after hatching]. This marks the point at which the gonads become fully functional and gametogenesis begins, though actual breeding is typically deferred for some time after this physiological landmark. The relatively early attainment of puberty relative to the overall lifespan suggests a strategy that allows young birds to begin scouting territories and forming pair bonds well before they invest in their first reproductive attempt. Histological examinations of gonadal tissue from captive individuals confirm that by this age, the testes in males contain mature spermatozoa and the ovaries in females possess developing follicles capable of ovulation. The endocrine triggers for this process are influenced by photoperiod and food availability, but the core developmental programme appears to be canalised under favourable thermal conditions. This age at puberty is comparable to that reported for other tropical dove species, which tend to mature faster than their temperate-zone relatives.

First reproduction occurs at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] when maintained at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This delay between physiological puberty and first breeding is common among columbids and is thought to reflect the time required for young adults to secure a suitable territory, establish a stable pair bond, and acquire the foraging experience necessary to sustain the energetic demands of egg production and chick rearing. The reproductive output during this first event is modest: females typically lay 1 egg per clutch [N_R_i = 1 egg per clutch], and produce only 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year]. This conservative strategy contrasts with the higher fecundity observed in some temperate dove species, which may produce multiple broods annually. The slow early reproductive rate may be linked to the Red collared dove's relatively high adult survival rate, favouring iteroparity over a high-risk, high-annual-output strategy. The annual reproductive effort is thus concentrated into a single, carefully provisioned offspring.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Red collared dove is 5.3 years [am = 5.3 years] under the same standard conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a figure derived from long-term banding studies of wild populations. This longevity places the species within the typical range for small to medium-sized columbids. The basal metabolic rate of adults measured at this temperature is 125.65 milliliters per hour [JOi = 125.65 milliliters per hour], reflecting the energetic cost of maintaining homeostasis in a bird of this size at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. The ultimate wet weight of adult females stabilises at 75 grams [Wwi = 75 grams], while males achieve a larger adult mass of 104 grams [Wwi = 104 grams], a difference that is consistent with the modest sexual dimorphism reported in the species. This mass difference may influence partitioning of roles during incubation and brooding. The combination of a single-egg clutch, a moderate lifespan, and a clear size dimorphism paints a picture of a species adapted to stable, resource-predictable environments where a slow-paced life history is favoured over high fecundity.
